transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-09
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Claire Nguyen (Redwood SE), Dana Morris (CTO, Oryx Health), Miguel Alvarez (ML Eng), Priya Singh (Security)

Summary: High-level discovery to understand Oryx Health's requirements for a HIPAA-sensitive clinical notes summarization feature. Discussed model options (open models vs hosted closed models), required context window (long clinical notes), multilingual support (English + Spanish), tool-calling for EHR lookups, and deployment constraints (VPC/on-prem concerns). Agreed POC and sample data sharing.

Topics: model choices, context length (>=64k tokens?), KV cache/prefix caching, dedicated vs hosted, HIPAA/KMS, latency vs cost tradeoffs, benchmark plan.

Action items (captured verbally): see metadata.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir from Redwood, and with me is Claire our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:06] Dana (Oryx): Doing good, thanks. A little under the weather but excited to talk through this.
[00:09] Miguel (Oryx): Hey, yeah, same. We've been waiting for wording on the model trade-offs.
[00:12] Claire (Redwood): Awesome. Quick agenda: we'll cover where you are today, production constraints, model candidate list, and then deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private) and an initial benchmark plan. Sound okay?
[00:21] Priya (Oryx): Yep, that's perfect. Security is a big part for us so we'll interject there.
[00:25] Samir: Great. Dana, maybe you can start with the user flow and high-level success criteria.
[00:29] Dana: Sure — so Oryx is building a clinical notes summarization product for care teams. The idea is auto-generate short action items and a bulleted summary from long encounter notes, also surface relevant meds and allergies. Accuracy is obviously critical, also must be PHI-safe, so HIPAA compliance and auditability are non-negotiable. Latency target is sub-800ms for single doc summarization at 512 token output, but throughput is relatively low — maybe 5 to 10 QPS average, spiky peaks up to 30 QPS during morning rounds.
[00:52] Miguel: Also, the notes can be very long — 20k to 60k tokens in some cases. We need models that can handle long context or we want a strategy to stitch context.
[01:00] Claire: Okay, long context — good flag. We usually see two approaches: use long-context models (some open models now support 64k windows) or use a retrieval+chunking pattern with KV/prefix caching to stitch. For your latency goals, long-window native models reduce complexity but often cost more.
[01:20] Dana: Right. We're also bilingual — English and Spanish notes. So multilingual performance is important, at least parity for Spanish clinical terminology.
[01:28] Priya: From security: we need VPC-only control plane or on-prem for some clients, KMS integration for key management, audit logs, and SOC2 plus HIPAA. We also want to ensure minimal PHI exposure during any external POC.
[01:41] Samir: Understood. Redwood has three deployment surfaces — Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC / on-prem). Hosted can be HIPAA-ready with BAAs and enterprise controls for some customers, but many enterprises prefer Dedicated or Private for full isolation. We can run the POC on Dedicated in a private subnet if that helps.
[01:58] Miguel: Can you clarify the difference between Dedicated and Private again? We've heard the terms but aren't sure about operational tradeoffs.
[02:03] Claire: Sure — Dedicated is Redwood-managed hardware reserved for you, isolated tenancy and predictable throughput; you still use our control plane but with network isolation and optional VPC peering. Private is customer-managed control plane for regulated setups — we can provide an appliance/on-prem package or a VPC deployment where the control plane is in your account. Private tends to have higher onboarding overhead but gives the most control for audits.
[02:27] Dana: Okay makes sense. Regarding models — what open models should we evaluate? We're trying to avoid vendor lock, prefer open weights but open to best-in-class closed models for a phase if needed.
[02:36] Claire: For long context + multilingual, candidates we've been seeing: Mistral Long forms (mis-named sometimes in notes as "Mistrel"), LlamaX variants with extended context, and specialized long-window models like LongLlama variants (these names sometimes get mangled in speech, sorry). For accuracy we also benchmark Anthropic/Claude and OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts-ish but of course those are closed APIs. On the open side, people test Mistral-Instruct, Redfern (internal shorthand), and some quantized Llama2/3 derivatives.
[03:05] Miguel: We're interested in native 64k context if it exists. Do you have concrete model sizes and token limits?
[03:11] Claire: Yes — a few options: a 32k native model (open), 64k experimental variants (some open, but often need patching/quantization to run economically). We also recommend a hybrid: use retrieval for older notes and full context for the most recent 8-10k tokens. That keeps average latency/cost down.
[03:29] Samir: Also note Redwood supports kv cache hot-paths and prefix caching which reduces repeated token cost when you're doing iterative summarization across a patient's notes. That can be a big cost saver.
[03:39] Priya: How does KV caching interact with PHI? Does caching keep raw text in memory or disk we need to encrypt?
[03:44] Claire: Good question. KV cache is in-memory by default and ephemeral; we offer encrypted-at-rest options for Dedicated and Private, with KMS integration. For Hosted you can enable stricter retention policies and ephemeral keys — we'll include the security doc with details.
[03:58] Dana: On the evaluation side — performance is important but we need quality metrics: factual accuracy, hallucination rates, and extraction precision for meds/allergy. Can Redwood help with automated evals?
[04:07] Claire: Yes — Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks; we can run regression tests on prompt sets and integrate your reference outputs. For POC we'll run quality and latency benchmarks side-by-side.
[04:15] Miguel: About tool-calling — we want the model to call an internal EHR API to fetch structured lab values or meds, then produce a combined summary. Is that supported?
[04:23] Samir: We support function/tool calling primitives similar to what folks see in other APIs. You can define structured tools (EHR get-labs, get-medications) and the model can call them; Redwood routes the tool call to your endpoint or to a mock during the POC. For on-prem/private we can keep those tool endpoints inside the network.
[04:40] Priya: Any limits on tool-calling for Dedicated v Hosted?
[04:44] Claire: No functional limits — it's more about network topology. Hosted routes outbound calls through our egress unless you use VPC peering/Private where calls can stay inside your network. For security-sensitive calls we'd recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC peering.
[04:57] Dana: Let's talk cost briefly — do you have rough per-1k-token numbers for long-window models vs chunking?
[05:02] Samir: Ballpark: large native long-window models can be 2–5x the per-token cost of 8k models due to memory and compute. Chunking + retrieval can reduce token cost but adds infra and latency. We'll share a cost-teardown spreadsheet after the call showing batch sizes, quantization, and amortized KV savings.
[05:18] Miguel: Do you support quantized runtimes? We plan to run some 4-bit quant models to lower cost.
[05:23] Claire: Yes — the runtime supports quantized weights and we've got quantization profiles that preserve peaks of quality depending on the model. For Dedicated/Private you can pin quantization variants.
[05:33] Dana: On latency, you said 800ms target for one doc. With a 32k window model, is that realistic?
[05:38] Claire: For a single GPU and a well-optimized kernel, 800ms for a 512-token output from a 32k context is aggressive but possible in Dedicated with batch size 1 and fast kernel paths — but it depends on sequence length distribution. For 64k window models latency will typically be higher. We usually recommend Dedicated for low-latency SLOs.
[05:56] Priya: For HIPAA, we need a BAA. Do you sign BAAs for Hosted?
[06:00] Samir: Yes, Redwood signs BAAs for enterprise customers. For customers with strict residency we recommend Dedicated/Private. We'll attach the legal pack.
[06:08] Miguel: Can we see example prompts and tuning you recommend for summarization of clinical notes?
[06:13] Claire: Absolutely. We'll include a prompt library and an initial prompt tuning recipe — few-shot + instructions + retrieval context works well. We can also run a small finetune or LoRA if you want to push medical accuracy, but that would change the evaluation axis and costs.
[06:30] Dana: A couple nitty-gritty items — do you persist logs? We need an audit trail for who invoked summaries and what model version was used.
[06:37] Samir: Redwood Console provides model-level and token-level audit trails, per-request metadata, and traces. For Private deployments you can forward logs to your SIEM/S3. We'll include screenshots.
[06:47] Miguel: On multilingual — Spanish clinical terms are tricky. Which open models have been strongest in medical Spanish?
[06:52] Claire: In our internal tests, some Spanish performance comes from larger Llama-family variants fine-tuned on Spanish corpora; Mistral has some promising multilingual variants too. We recommend starting with a multilingual open model and doing targeted evals on Spanish prompts — if necessary, add a small in-domain fine-tune or adapter.
[07:09] Dana: About tooling: we need structured outputs (JSON) for downstream ingestion. Do you support strict output schemas and validation?
[07:15] Claire: Yes, Redwood supports structured output constraints and can run output validators. We also support function-calling which naturally produces structured responses. We'll give examples.
[07:24] Samir: Quick question to the group — what would success for the POC look like? Is it a quality threshold, latency, or a combination?
[07:29] Miguel: Combination. At least 85% extraction precision for meds/allergy on a 200-case test set, and average latency under 1s, cost within X (we'll provide a target).
[07:39] Priya: And security sign-off on the infra and BAA.
[07:42] Dana: Also reproducible model behavior — we need to be able to audit a few tricky cases.
[07:47] Claire: Good. We'll design the benchmark to capture these metrics — precision/recall, hallucination rate, per-case latency, and cost per doc.
[07:56] Samir: For the POC environment, would you prefer we spin up Dedicated for the benchmark or start Hosted with stricter controls?
[08:02] Dana: For initial convos we can start Hosted to move quickly if the BAA is in place, but for the actual benchmark we want Dedicated. That way we see predictable latency under committed capacity.
[08:13] Miguel: Agreed, Dedicated for the benchmark, Hosted for some exploratory work might be okay.
[08:17] Priya: If you start Hosted, we need assurance that the data used is encrypted and not persisted beyond the session.
[08:22] Samir: We'll make that explicit in the pack. Claire, do you want to talk about benchmark plan?
[08:26] Claire: Sure — propose: 1) Redwood runs initial quality/VOC check on a 200-case de-identified set; 2) run throughput/latency benchmark on Dedicated with 1, 5, 30 QPS profiles; 3) run Spanish-specific subset; 4) run tool-calling integration scenario. We'll provide scripts and a link to a shared spreadsheet for results.
[08:47] Miguel: Timing? We can provision the de-id data by next week.
[08:50] Claire: Great. We can schedule the benchmark window 2027-09-15 as Samir suggested earlier.
[08:55] Dana: Who will own the security review? Priya will lead from our side.
[08:58] Priya: Yep, I'll coordinate. We'll also want the SOC2 report and architecture diagram.
[09:03] Samir: We'll attach SOC2, the HIPAA pack, and an architecture playbook for VPC and on-prem.
[09:10] Miguel: A quick technical question — how do you handle model rollouts and version pinning? If we fine-tune or use LoRA, can we pin a variant to traffic?
[09:17] Claire: Yes — Redwood Console supports model versioning and rollout policies (canary, A/B, and automatic fallback). You can pin traffic to a specific model variant in Dedicated/Private. For Hosted we also support pinning but some variants may require dedicated infra.
[09:29] Dana: Any gotchas with tokenizer differences across models for clinical abbreviations?
[09:33] Claire: Good point — tokenization differences can affect prompt engineering and cost. We'll include tokenizer stats for candidate models and a sample tokenizer preview tool.
[09:42] Miguel: Do you provide tooling for k-v cache debugging? We had issues where cache invalidation caused stale summaries.
[09:48] Claire: We have tracing hooks in the runtime to inspect KV state and cache hit rates, plus TTL controls. We'll show sample traces in the POC run.
[09:58] Priya: For encryption: do you have HSM/KMS options for keys and also a key rotation policy?
[10:03] Samir: Yes — we integrate with common cloud KMS providers and can support customer-managed keys in Dedicated/Private. Rotation policies can be applied and we log key use for audits.
[10:12] Dana: Can we talk about integration patterns for EHR tool-calling — specifically how to authenticate the model gateway to EHR APIs?
[10:18] Claire: We support service accounts and signed JWTs; for Private you can present the model runtime within your network and use existing enterprise auth. For Hosted we can proxy calls through a secure egress with mTLS to your endpoints.
[10:31] Miguel: Are there any limitations on attachments like images in notes? We might have photos or ECG snippets.
[10:36] Samir: Redwood is developing multimodal support; for now most clinical-image work is a separate pipeline. We can handle basic multimodal via separate pre-processing and structured inputs, but true joint vision-language is still in early access.
[10:51] Dana: Okay. Any objections to doing a small LoRA if the base model underperforms on Spanish?
[10:56] Claire: Not at all — LoRA is an option, but we should weigh reproducibility and governance. LoRAs can be pinned in the model registry and audited like other artifacts.
[11:05] Miguel: For the benchmark, what metrics will you report?
[11:08] Claire: We'll report extraction precision/recall for meds/allergies, ROUGE/L for summary overlap, hallucination flags (manually reviewed subset), per-request latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), and cost per 1k output tokens.
[11:20] Priya: We also need retention policy for logs — can we enforce 30-day auto-deletion for Hosted POC?
[11:24] Samir: Yes we can set retention windows per tenant during POC. For Dedicated/Private you control retention.
[11:31] Dana: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[11:34] Samir: Recap: Redwood will share POC pricing spreadsheet, HIPAA/security pack, and proposed benchmark scripts + prompt library. You'll share de-identified sample and target QPS, and Priya will schedule a security review. We set a tentative benchmark for 2027-09-15.
[11:52] Miguel: Correct. Also Claire will prepare the test prompts and Spanish subset.
[11:55] Priya: I'll send a list of security questions and the contacts for our Infosec.
[11:59] Dana: Timeline-wise, if POC goes well we aim to go live with a limited beta in Q4 2027.
[12:06] Claire: Sounds good. I'll also include a short technical note on expected latency tradeoffs for 32k vs 64k models and the cost impacts.
[12:14] Samir: Any final questions?
[12:17] Dana: Not from me. Thanks for the clear plan.
[12:20] Miguel: No, thanks.
[12:22] Priya: All good.
[12:24] Samir: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and book the benchmark slot.
[12:28] (meeting ends)
